news.title: Where Is The US Support For The Guyana Ferry Disaster?  - Antigua Tribune – Daily Antigua & Caribbean
news.text:
News Americas, NEW YORK, NY, Fri. July 24, 2026: Just days after US officials stood in Washington promising to help lead Guyana’s energy and infrastructure future, the country was hit by one of its worst maritime disasters in decades. So where has that promised American partnership been in the recovery?

As the MV Barima death toll climbed past 72 this week, the US response has amounted to a single social media post from Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and a statement from the US Embassy in Guyana, both offering condolences. Neither US President Donald Trump nor Secretary of State Marco Rubio has personally commented on the disaster. No US personnel, vessels or equipment have been reported as part of the search and recovery operation.

Compare that to the countries that sent people and equipment into the water. France deployed a 15-member military team from French Guiana, including 12 specialist divers, two medics and a mechanic, to join the search. Trinidad and Tobago’s Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar announced her government had mobilized air and naval assets along with Trinidad and Tobago Defence Force personnel, including a Coast Guard vessel. Brazil’s navy joined the recovery effort as well, assisting with diving missions at the wreck site. Even the CARICOM Private Sector Organisation pledged to stand ready to assist.

China’s response has mirrored Washington’s: the Chinese Embassy in Guyana said it was “closely following” the search and extended sympathy, but has not been reported as providing personnel or equipment either. The European Union, Canada and the United Kingdom similarly offered only condolences.

Just last week, Deputy Secretary Landau himself addressed a US-Guyana Investment Enabling Forum in Washington, where officials described positioning American companies to “lead in energy, infrastructure, and other sectors central to” Guyana’s growth as a strategic priority. That rhetoric of partnership and American commitment to Guyana’s future has not translated into operational support during the country’s actual moment of need.

Guyana holds one of the fastest-growing oil economies in the world, and Washington has spent months courting a deeper commercial relationship with Georgetown, paired with public reassurances about respecting the country’s sovereignty. Whether that relationship extends to showing up when Guyana is drowning, literally, is a question this week has left unanswered.

For those families facing the grueling task of burying their dead, including Rachel Wells’ surviving husband, now left to bury his wife and their three children, Nathaniel Jr., 8, Natalia, 5, and Ezekiel, 3, the US silence is mind-numbing. Even ExxonMobil, so often accused of profiting quietly off Guyana’s oil wealth while giving little back, moved faster than Washington, redirecting all ticket proceeds from next month’s Guyana Amazon Warriors Super League final to victims’ families. Washington sent a condolence post.

news.title: Everyday Revolutionary War heroes take center stage in Trump’s ‘Spirit of ‘76’ exhibit
news.text:
EXCLUSIVE: Beneath a towering 23-foot bronze figure holding the Declaration of Independence aloft, designer Matthew Taylor stopped beside an equestrian statue that many Americans have likely never seen, or even heard of.

“Most Americans have never heard of Caesar Rodney,” Taylor told Fox News Digital during an exclusive tour of the new Spirit of ’76 exhibition at Freedom Plaza. “But we owe this man an enormous debt of gratitude.”

The temporary installation, unveiled as part of America’s 250th anniversary celebration, transforms Freedom Plaza into an open-air gallery honoring Revolutionary War figures whose names rarely appear in history textbooks.

Commissioned by President Donald Trump, the exhibition features 22 statues and sculptural installations, including a restored equestrian monument of Rodney, a towering “Spirit of Liberty” centerpiece, bronze figures representing Revolutionary soldiers, and an immersive memorial honoring Americans who died aboard British prison ships during the Revolution.

According to the National Park Service, the exhibit was created to honor the “heroes and martyrs of the Revolution” during America’s semiquincentennial and is intended to celebrate the enduring “Spirit of ’76’ that continues to live on in every American heart.” 

The centerpiece installations include the Caesar Rodney equestrian statue, the “12 Soldiers of the Revolution,” the Prison Ship Martyrs memorial and the 23-foot Spirit of Liberty statue.

Rather than beginning with George Washington or Thomas Jefferson, however, Taylor chose to introduce visitors to Rodney.

The Delaware statesman, one of the signers of the Declaration of Independence, is remembered for his legendary overnight ride from Dover to Philadelphia in July 1776. Suffering from severe illness, Rodney rode roughly 80 miles through a storm to cast the vote that broke Delaware’s deadlock in favor of independence.

“Of all the signers of the Declaration of Independence, Caesar Rodney is one of the most exciting,” Taylor said. “When Delaware’s delegation was deadlocked, he rode through the night to cast the vote that helped secure American independence.”

For decades, the bronze statue stood in Wilmington’s Rodney Square before being removed in 2020. It now occupies one of the most prominent locations in the nation’s capital, just blocks from both the White House and the Capitol.

From Rodney’s ride, Taylor naturally guides visitors into the next chapter of the American story.

Arranged around the plaza are bronze sculptures representing 12 Revolutionary War soldiers. Rather than depicting famous generals, the statues celebrate ordinary Americans whose individual stories reflect the sacrifices of the Revolutionary generation.

“These are ordinary citizens who did extraordinary things,” Taylor said. “Every one of these statues tells the story of someone who answered the call during the Revolution.”

Among them is Samuel Whittemore, who fought British troops at age 78. According to Taylor, Whittemore was bayoneted multiple times, shot in the head and left for dead before surviving and living into his 90s.

Another figure, Simon Knowles, enlisted at just 15 years old and served alongside George Washington throughout much of the Revolutionary War before returning home to live as a farmer.

Taylor said those stories represent the exhibition’s central message.

“Unlike monuments to George Washington or Thomas Jefferson, these statues honor ordinary Americans who did extraordinary things,” he said.

Nearby, another installation tells one of the Revolution’s lesser-known tragedies.

Designed as visitors physically walk through its narrow bronze panels, the Prison Ship Martyrs memorial recreates the outline of a British prison ship. According to the National Park Service, nearly 12,000 Americans died aboard prison ships during the Revolutionary War; even more than were killed in combat during the conflict.

Taylor said the memorial is meant to immerse visitors in that experience.

“As you walk inside, you hear the water from the fountain,” he explained during the tour. “It helps place you inside the story.”

The fountain itself has also become part of the experience. Taylor noted it was recently restored to operation after years of sitting idle, providing the soundscape surrounding the memorial while complementing the plaza’s redesign.

Towering above the entire exhibition stands the Spirit of Liberty, a new bronze figure inspired by iconic American monuments while looking toward the country’s next 250 years.

Standing 23 feet tall, the statue holds an exact bronze replica of the Declaration of Independence in one hand while raising a sword skyward with the other. Around its base are reliefs depicting three defining moments of the Revolution: the signing of the Declaration of Independence, George Washington crossing the Delaware River and the British surrender at Yorktown.

“The Spirit of Liberty represents the sacrifices that gave birth to this nation,” Taylor said.

During Fox News Digital’s visit, visitors gathered around the plaza to photograph the statues against the Washington skyline. Low-angle views of the bronze figures framed them against bright summer skies, while Rodney’s horse appeared frozen mid-stride as though continuing the historic ride that helped shape the nation’s founding.

For Taylor, whose career has largely been spent both behind the camera and behind the scenes designing historical works, the exhibition is about more than commemorating famous names.

Instead, he hopes visitors leave thinking about people they had never encountered before arriving at Freedom Plaza.

“When visitors leave here,” Taylor said, “I hope they realize they can do extraordinary things themselves. America was built by ordinary citizens who answered extraordinary moments.”

The Spirit of ’76 exhibition is free to the public and is scheduled to remain on display throughout the nation’s 250th anniversary celebration.
news.summary: Designer Matthew Taylor says the Spirit of '76 exhibition celebrates ordinary citizens who did extraordinary things
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Top North Korea official blasts Asean for urging denuclearisation
news.text: SEOUL, South Korea — The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attacked the bloc of Southeast Asian nations on Monday for seeking a denuclearised Korean peninsula, blasting the position as 'stupid and foolish.'At its annual regional forum last week, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) expressed 'grave concern' over Pyongyang's ongoing nuclear weapons development and stressed the importance of dialogue 'to realise lasting peace and stability in a denuclearised Korean Peninsula.'North Korea has long insisted on its right to nuclear weapon and ballistic missile programmes, although they are forbidden under the terms of UN Security Council sanctions. It enshrined its nuclear status in its constitution in 2023.Kim's sister Kim Yo Jong said in a statement carried by state news outlet KCNA that she expressed 'strong dissatisfaction with the forum's undisguised hostile attitude of going along with the US trumpeting about 'denuclearisation'' and ignoring North Korea's constitution.'It is a failure in strategic thinking and logic and a manifestation of a stupid and foolish wild dream to still adhere to the 'denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula' which had already lost its meaning conceptually and practically,' she said.ASEAN should guard against 'being misused as a hired mouthpiece for the US,' she added.In June, Kim Yo Jong -- a key player in the North's communications and foreign policy -- said in a statement that North Korea's nuclear weapons programme is 'the line of no retreat'.Pyongyang has repeatedly declared itself an 'irreversible' nuclear state since Kim Jong Un's 2019 summit with US President Donald Trump collapsed over the scope of denuclearisation and sanctions relief.

news.title: Miranda Devine: Anthony Fauci was the ‘big head’ of COVID response
news.text:
The vanity of Anthony Fauci will be his undoing.

Until now, the deceitful health bureaucrat’s reputation has remained intact despite damning revelations about his attempted cover-up of the origins of COVID-19, suspected involvement in outsourcing dangerous research on bat viruses to China and mishandling of the pandemic.

But, days before Fauci has to again face his nemesis, Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, on Capitol Hill, his excruciatingly embarrassing diary entries have turned him into a laughingstock.

In a bombshell data dump Saturday, Paul, chairman of the Senate’s oversight committee, which will grill Fauci under oath on Wednesday, released what he said was Fauci’s diary from December 2019 through December 2022.

“What he wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories,” tweeted Paul, who has long accused Fauci of being involved in the virus’ creation.

Fauci emerges from the diary entries as a frivolous narcissist, possibly corrupt and a really bad speller (for example, “dyswaded” for dissuaded).

As the global death toll mounted, Fauci’s diary shows he was increasingly preoccupied with his rising media profile and reveling in the admiration, especially the praise from celebrities, all of which he meticulously -recorded.

‘Flattered’ by praise

“Much praise for me,” he gushed on March 4, 2020, after recording 108 cases of coronavirus in the US and 10 deaths.

“Everyone in the WH is congratulating me on the piece [fawning Politico profile of Fauci]. The public adulation of me has been amazing with every young intern as well as seasoned veteran in the WH coming over to me congratulating me and thanking me for my work and even asking for selfies.”

On March 15, 2020, he wrote: “BIG DAY!… USA = 2888 [cases] with 58 deaths . . . I did all 5 Sunday Shows today (my 3rd Fauci 5) with This Week on ABC, Meet the Press on NBC, Face the Nation on CBS, FOX with Chris Wallace and CNN.”

Day after day he recorded the praise, the media profiles, the “multiple TV cameras and hundreds of camera clicks follow[ing] me,” and his centrality in the decision-making at the White House in those early days of the -pandemic.

“I spoke with Bill de Blasio (Mayor – NYC) and convinced him based on what I was saying publicly and my conversation tonight to close the NYC schools. I went on to tell him he should close the bars and restaurants in NYC. He said that he would base this on my recommendation.”

“Big front page article abut [sic] me appeared in the Washington Post. Very flattering,” he wrote on May 21, 2020, noting global deaths of 9,800, with 272 deaths in the US.

“It is not hyoperbole [sic] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable peson [sic] in the world . . . The entire secret service corps is coming over to me and chatting. They let me into the first gate without even checking ID.”

May 23, 2020, after cases shot up 20 percent overnight: “Apparently the WH is very upset that I am being profiled and it looks like I am putting down the POTUS and becoming a star that outshines him.”

After the November 2020 election, he was less diligent about noting the death toll, which was higher under his pal Joe Biden than Donald Trump. But he had plenty of room to record praise from celebrities.

“Praised by Barbara Bush in an interview and several celebrities.

“[Billionaire] Adrienne Arsht sent me an amazing video [the Kennedy Center] put together to celebrate my 80th birthday. They gathered a whole bunch of celebrities to sing to me and offer words of praise and congratulations: Orlando Bloom, Mila Kunis and Ashton Kutcher, Amy Poehler, Lily Tomlin, Sophia Bush, Matthew McConaughey, Steve Buscemi, Magic Johnson, Joan Baez, and many others.”

Oh yes, there were many others, all faithfully recorded in his name-dropping diary:

Barbra Streisand sent a note expressing deep appreciation for his “important and consistent work.”

Julia Roberts called him her “personal hero.”

Every week, Post columnist Miranda Devine sits down for exclusive and candid conversations with the most influential disruptors in Washington on ‘Pod Force One.’ Subscribe here!

Joe and Jill Biden sent “cookies + note” from the basement in March 2020, saying: “You are our hero. Stay strong and healthy. We need you.”

Dick Cheney called to thank him. Then-VP Mike Pence told him he is “the most visible and trusted asset in the country.”

By June 2022, he was officially a legend: “It has been an extraordinary spring with all of these wonderful honors that I have received. This will have been my 58th honorary doctorate.”

When he announced he was retiring as Biden’s adviser in August 2022, Fauci records the praise from Biden chief of staff Ron Klain: “he considers me ‘one of the most important public servants in the history of the country’ given that I have saved millions of lives over the last several years . . .

“The number of texts and e-mail of thanks and praise . . . are stunning.”

“I am really being somewhat embarrassed by the amount of honors that are [being] given to me and kudos my way.”

In November 2022, he records a “Terrific event,” at which “I was honored at the home of the French Ambassador . . . They sang my praises and we had a very elegant dinner . . . Photo shoot at my home and at work by prize-winning (MOMA) photojournalist Wolfgang Tillmans.”

All those Fauci bobbleheads and “In Fauci we trust” bumper stickers and shrines to the left’s favorite health fascist clearly didn’t help him with his humility problem.

Such is the insatiable nature of vanity that the more adulation he received the more he craved.

The hubris first exploded into public in his 2024 memoir, “On Call: A Doctor’s Journey in Public Service,” described by National Review as “insufferably vain — the book lovingly records a seemingly endless torrent of compliments from celebrities, colleagues, and employees.”

Other reviews noted its “vainglorious self-promotion” and said Fauci “has no trouble remembering every bit of praise that others have heaped upon him.”

This is how Fauci described his career at the National Institutes of Health, where he began in 1964 straight out of medical school and rose to be head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases: “My upward career trajectory was steep. I was becoming well-known and respected nationally and internationally . . . someone who had the explicit respect of and thus access to the highest leaders of government.”

Deified himself

Additional files released by Paul in the prelude to Wednesday’s showdown reveal that Fauci, who had been the highest-paid federal official in the US government, also solicited nominations for big-money awards for himself from scientists to whom he had given millions in government grants, according to the files.

He “stacked up cash prizes worth hundreds of thousands of dollars during COVID,” said Paul, including one foreign prize worth a cool $900,000.

Fauci even had his taxpayer-funded staff writing nominations for him.

“Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall,” warns the Bible about such hubris.

But his 50 years as a powerful bureaucrat taught Fauci only that he was a god; and after all the damage he wrought, it’s hardly consolation to witness his inevitable fall.

It is simply a tragedy that a man so flawed could wield such power.
news.summary: The vanity of Anthony Fauci will be his undoing.
news.author: Miranda Devine

news.title: Oil prices slip 5% after US-Iran pause strikes, lifting supply hopes
news.text: Oil prices tumbled 5 per cent on Monday after the US and Iran paused strikes over the weekend after two ​weeks of attacks, raising hopes of a diplomatic solution ​that would de-escalate the conflict and allow shipping to resume in the ‌Strait of Hormuz.Brent crude futures fell $4.89, or 5.05 per cent, to $91.89 by 0009 GMT after briefly slipping under the key support level of $90 earlier in the session.US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $84.64 a barrel, down $4.67, or 5.23 per cent.Both contracts are trading at their lowest levels in nearly a week after rising for the past three weeks.Brent had reached $100 per barrel as the conflict, which reduced oil shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, spilled over to the Red Sea, hindering exports from the world's top exporter, Saudi Arabia, via ‌the Bab el-Mandeb strait to Asia.The US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told "Fox News Sunday" and other US media that President Donald Trump had decided to pause US attacks to allow more time for diplomacy."Hopes are rising that a genuine diplomatic path may be opening," IG markets analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note."A return to the 14-point MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a ​little more clarity around control of the Strait of Hormuz would be a solid starting point."Despite ‌the pause in attacks, fewer than 10 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz daily during the weekend, shipping data from Kpler ​showed.In addition, ‌ship traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb strait fell on Sunday after Yemeni Houthis attacked ‌Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast, although a third Chinese supertanker exited via the Bab el-Mandeb strait."Any rebound in flows through the Strait ‌of ​Hormuz is likely ​to prove slow and partial, as many shippers remain wary and will want greater confidence in their safety before they bring more empty ‌ships into the ​Strait," MST Marquee analyst Saul Kavonic said.

news.title: Oil prices fall 5%: Crude cools as US-Iran pause fuels hopes of diplomatic breakthrough
news.text: Oil prices tumbled sharply on Monday after the United States and Iran held back from launching fresh strikes over the weekend, raising hopes that diplomacy could ease tensions in the Middle East and gradually restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Brent crude futures were down $4.37, or 4.52%, at $92.41 a barrel after slipping 5.05% earlier. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was also 5.23% down before trading $4.30, or 4.81%, lower at $85.01 a barrel around 7:15 am. Both benchmark contracts traded at their lowest levels in nearly a week, retreating after three consecutive weeks of gains.In early trading on Sunday, Brent crude for September delivery fell 4.9% to $92.02 a barrel after reopening, extending a 3.9% decline recorded on Friday. Benchmark US crude for September delivery dropped 5.6% to $84.34 after falling 3.1% in the previous session. Meanwhile, Brent crude for October delivery, now the most actively traded contract, declined 4.6% to $87.48.The decline came after the US and Iran refrained from carrying out military strikes in the Persian Gulf for a second straight day. The pause in hostilities followed two weeks of attacks and fuelled hopes that a diplomatic solution could help de-escalate the conflict.US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told Fox News Sunday and other US media that Donald Trump had decided to pause US attacks to allow more time for diplomacy."Hopes are rising that a genuine diplomatic path may be opening," IG Markets analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note."A return to the 14-point MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a little more clarity around control of the Strait of Hormuz would be a solid starting point."Brent crude had climbed as high as $100 a barrel during the recent escalation, while it briefly touched $102 last week, its highest level since May and around $30 above the most actively traded Brent contract earlier in the month. The surge was driven by intensified fighting in the Middle East and concerns that a wider conflict would further disrupt global crude supplies.Shipping disruptions continueDespite the pause in attacks, shipping through key trade routes remained subdued.Shipping data from Kpler showed that fewer than 10 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day over the weekend. Traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also declined on Sunday after Yemeni Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast, although a third Chinese supertanker managed to exit through the waterway.The Strait of Hormuz has remained the focal point for oil markets since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Around a fifth of the world's oil typically passes through the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf to global markets, but the conflict has largely halted shipping traffic. Oil producers have sought alternative routes, though those have also come under pressure following attacks on Saudi oil tankers using the Red Sea.Although oil prices have retreated from last week's highs, uncertainty continues to linger over the conflict and its impact on energy markets. However, even with this steep rise, prices continue to be lower than the $126 per barrel mark reached earlier during the conflict.Get the latest Business News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

news.title: World News | Nearly 3,00,000 Evacuated as Wildfires Advance Toward Bordeaux in France and Devastate Central Spain
news.text:
Bordeaux [France], July 27 (ANI): Uncontrolled wildfires advanced toward the outer edge of Bordeaux on Sunday, pushing into the heart of France's winemaking region as emergency crews across France and Spain struggled to contain blazes that have forced roughly 3,00,000 people to flee from their homes.

According to France 24, authorities reported that roughly 220,000 people have been evacuated across France. In neighbouring Spain, over 75,000 residents have been forced to flee, while another 30,000 have been instructed to shelter in place.

Also Read | Donald Trump Shares AI-Generated Images of Strike on Kharg Island, Issues Fresh Warning to Iran.

France 24 reported that French firefighters are working to prevent the flames from breaching Bordeaux's regional capital after blazes swept through the popular Atlantic coast tourist destination of the Cap Ferret peninsula and spread through the surrounding countryside.

Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave noted that the main firefront was positioned approximately 15 kilometres (9 miles) from the city's primary entry points. While earlier stating there were no immediate plans to evacuate the city--whose broader metropolitan area holds a population of roughly 850,000, Cazenave acknowledged the proximity of the threat.

Also Read | 'Cannot Go Unanswered': Abbas Araghchi Condemns Ukraine's Caspian Sea Strike on Iranian Vessel.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Sunday underscored the severity of the crisis.

"We have a fire that is not under control and which is moving in the direction of the city area," Nunez stated, adding, "The overall situation is very unfavourable, we are in a situation that is unprecedented," Nunez affirmed that officials would continue to monitor and evaluate the situation realistically.

As the firefront pressed closer, French authorities released footage showing police officers conducting door-to-door overnight evacuations in the municipalities of Marcheprime and Cestas, knocking on doors in the dark to urge families to evacuate immediately, France 24 reported.

Cross-border efforts are also intensifying in Spain, where Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited fire-ravaged areas in Avila, one of three central provinces, alongside Madrid and Toledo, confronting major blazes.

According to Spanish Environment Minister Sara Aagesen, flames have destroyed more than 50,000 hectares (123,500 acres) of land in Avila alone, marking it as the largest wildfire in Spain's recent history.

France 24 further reported on a separate, uncontained blaze in eastern Spain's Castellon province that has burned over 4,300 hectares and spread into the Sierra de Espadan natural park, threatening extensive pine and cork oak forests.

"The fire is out of control, it's very difficult to extinguish from a technical standpoint, especially because of the adverse weather conditions that will continue throughout the day," Valencian regional leader Juanfran Perez told reporters near the scene.

International support is mobilising under the European Union's civil protection mechanism. Greece and Italy have each dispatched two Canadair firefighting aircraft to Spain, while Portugal has deployed over 100 military personnel alongside specialised equipment.

Spain's interior ministry announced on social media platform X that two additional aircraft from Turkey are expected to arrive as soon as possible.

Prime Minister Sanchez announced that his government will officially declare a civil protection emergency on Tuesday for the impacted central provinces, releasing recovery funds to assist affected communities.

Sanchez revealed that more than 150,000 hectares have been destroyed across Spain since January, a figure six times higher than the total area burned during the same timeframe last year, according to France 24. (ANI)

news.title: Six Networks: Inside China’s trillion-dollar bet to wire its economy for an AI era
news.text:
BEIJING – As competition with the US for technological dominance intensifies, China is embarking on a multi-trillion-dollar infrastructure push aimed at laying the foundations for long-term growth in an era it expects to be shaped by artificial intelligence.

Beijing is betting that success will not solely depend on advanced chips and AI models, but also on the physical systems that support them – from power grids and data centres to telecommunications networks and logistics.

The initiative, known as the Six Networks, is part of Beijing’s latest Five-Year Plan.

It marks the first time China has brought its biggest infrastructure projects under a single, integrated programme, rather than developing transport, energy and communications networks separately. 

As well as supporting the country’s AI ambitions, the government hopes the project will strengthen China’s manufacturing base, bolster resilience to geopolitical tensions, economic shocks and natural disasters, and advance the transition to a low-carbon economy. 

What is the Six Networks? 

The Six Networks is a national infrastructure programme to upgrade China’s vast physical and digital systems.

Scheduled for completion by 2030, it spans six areas: electricity, water, telecommunications, computing, logistics and underground pipe networks. China Securities estimates the project will cost more than 26 trillion yuan (S$5 trillion).

A central focus is digital infrastructure. China plans to build high-performance supercomputing centres, general purpose data centres and AI-focused compute hubs, as well as develop new ultra-high-speed fibre broadband, satellite internet and a sixth-generation, or 6G, mobile network. 

The electricity grid is also to be upgraded.

Beijing plans to expand long-distance transmission lines, strengthen urban and rural networks, and build more energy storage facilities to absorb renewable power.

It also plans to develop an AI-powered dispatch system capable of monitoring the grid in real time, adjusting power flows and matching renewable energy supply with data centre demand.

The project also includes an upgrade to transport and water infrastructure.

Logistics networks are set to have improved connections between production sites, ports and distribution hubs.

As part of the plan, existing flood-control systems – such as embankments, dykes and reservoirs – will be improved, while diversion projects that shift water from wet basins to arid areas and large irrigation districts will be expanded.

Finally, the government plans to build 770,000km of water, drainage, gas and heating pipelines beneath Chinese cities to replace ageing infrastructure, reduce leaks and flooding, and support urban development.

Why is China investing so heavily in the Six Networks?

Competition with the US over AI has made infrastructure a strategic priority for Beijing.

As AI models become larger and more sophisticated, they require enormous amounts of computing power and electricity, cooling water, high-speed communications networks and efficient supply chains.

Rather than treating those needs separately, China wants to build an integrated system.

Much of the attention has focused on the computing and telecommunications networks.

The government wants to connect scattered data processing hubs across the country through high-speed, stable networks, creating a nationally coordinated system that can direct AI workloads to whichever data centres have spare capacity – similar to how electricity flows through a power grid.

Officials also expect the network to underpin a wide range of AI uses, from factory automation and self-driving cars to robots.

Electricity is another piece of the puzzle.

New transmission lines and renewable energy projects are intended to provide abundant, low-cost clean power to data centres, whose power consumption is almost the equivalent to twice the annual output of the Three Gorges Dam – the world’s largest hydropower project by installed capacity.

Expanding the adoption of renewable energy would also advance Beijing’s carbon-neutral goals while bolstering energy security.

Other parts of the Six Networks plan support broader economic priorities.

Improvements to the logistics network are designed to reduce transport costs and better connect demand in China’s large, populous cities with supply from the farthest mountainous areas.

The water initiatives are aimed at strengthening food security and resilience against floods and droughts.

The hope is that modernising underground pipe networks should improve living conditions and also create construction work at a time when China is in the midst of a property downturn.

How will China pay for the Six Networks?

The cost of the project is expected to be nearly 50 per cent more than the combined investment across those six sectors during the last Five-Year Plan from 2021 to 2025, according to estimates by China Securities.

Public interest infrastructure, such as flood control systems and water diversion initiatives, is expected to be funded mainly through the issuance of central and local government bonds, alongside lending from policy banks – state-owned lenders that finance projects aligned with Beijing’s strategic priorities. 

Revenue-generating projects, including logistics hubs, are expected to attract private capital through public-private partnerships.

For underground pipelines, for example, investors may be granted operating concession rights that enable them to earn recurring revenue after the projects are completed. 

More commercially viable projects – including power, computing and communication networks – are expected to rely primarily on market-based corporate investment. 

Can China really deliver this?

China has a strong track record of delivering major projects under its five-year plans.

Large amounts of public money are set aside every year for such initiatives, and approvals for land and other resources are often fast-tracked.

Local officials also have strong incentives to ensure projects are completed, as their performance reviews and promotion prospects can be tied to how quickly and effectively they deliver them.

That said, financing could be a challenge this time.

Economic growth has slowed as consumer spending remains weak amid a soft job market and a prolonged real estate slump, weighing on corporate profits and investment.

Local governments, which have traditionally shouldered much of the cost of infrastructure spending, have also seen income from land sales shrink to less than half of its 2021 peak.

At the same time, Beijing has tightened limits on their borrowing as it tries to contain risks from the huge stockpile of off-balance-sheet debt that has accumulated since the Global Financial Crisis. 

Technology restrictions could also complicate the project. US-led export controls have limited China’s access to cutting-edge semiconductors, potentially slowing progress on the computing and communications networks at the heart of the project.

Another challenge will be the bureaucracy and coordination required for a project that spans multiple sectors.

Government researchers have warned that isolated planning across different government departments, inconsistent technical standards, and unclear benefit-sharing rules could lead to overlapping investment and undermine the project’s success. 

Is the US also ramping up its AI infrastructure?

Silicon Valley is betting that physical infrastructure is key to building more advanced AI systems and keeping ahead of China in the race for AI dominance.

Top US tech firms, including Meta Platforms, Alphabet’s Google and Amazon.com, plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars to build sprawling new data centres stocked with cutting-edge AI chips.

OpenAI’s Sam Altman has previously said he expects his firm to spend “trillions” on infrastructure to develop and run AI. 

The US government has thrown its support behind this push.

The Trump administration has previously unveiled plans to use federal land and resources to build data centres, and steps to ensure there is enough power to run energy-hungry AI data centres.

Not all policymakers are on board, however. A growing number of local and state officials have taken tougher stances on data centre development, following a surge in community pushback over the impacts on utility prices and the environment. 

New York Governor Kathy Hochul recently announced a one-year moratorium on new large data centre projects in the state.

President Donald Trump responded by calling it a “terrible decision”.

“Data centres are tremendous Wins for the states and communities that are lucky enough to get them,” he wrote in a social media post. BLOOMBERG

news.title: US lowers Iran war deaths from 18 to 14 after Pentagon changes how it reports casualties
news.text: The US Pentagon has revised the casualty figures for Operation Epic Fury, bringing down the number of troops listed as killed from 18 to 14 and removing dozens of wounded service members from the tally after it abruptly updated its public casualty database last week.In its Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), the Defense Department appears to be tracking casualties under a new category labeled "Overseas Operations" rather than "Operation Epic Fury," the previously used name for the military campaign in Iran, effectively resetting its accounting of the war's dead and wounded, ABC News reported Monday.Pentagon lowers Iran war casualties, fatalities: What we knowWhile the public casualty database has previously posted shifting casualty figures since the war began in February, the discrepancies peaked on 23 July, when the reported death toll fell to 14, removing the four US service members killed in Jordan and Iraq recently.Additionally, the number of wounded troops also dropped from 482 on 22 July to 420 on 23 July. The revised figures appear to be in contrast with the Pentagon's own statement released last week, in which spokesperson Sean Parnell noted that roughly 100 additional troops had been wounded since 7 July, when the two sides resumed hostilities.The changes are reflected in the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), which is the Pentagon's primary public database for tracking the country's military casualties. DCAS is maintained using data submitted by the military services and serves as the federal government's official public record of war casualties.However, it remains unclear how the Defense Department and its officials are defining "overseas operations" and whether it is exclusively counting casualties and fatalities from the Iran war.The department's decision to separate individual phases of the war from the broader campaign is unprecedented and could make it harder to determine the total number of US military casualties, the report added. Further, the new Overseas Operations category also includes 207 troops wounded since 7 July, marking at least 624 members as injured since the US and Israel launched the war.The revised accounting may be tied to US President Donald Trump's administration's view that Operation Epic Fury ended in May, with the renewed fighting resetting the 60-day limit for military action without congressional approval.Lawmakers slam Trump admin over reduced casualties countThe database, which continues to undercount the conflict's casualties, with Defense Department officials attributing the discrepancies to a technical issue, has received massive backlash, further raising questions about the department's underlying system for tracking casualties.The revised casualty reporting has drawn criticism from lawmakers, who argue that the administration is making the Iran war's casualty figures less transparent while attempting to bypass the 60-day limit on military action without congressional approval by treating the conflict as a new operation.Last week, Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to clarify the Pentagon's casualty reporting and called for a "full and accurate accounting" of all service members killed or wounded since the start of the Iran war.New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "outraged" to see that the name of Sgt. Angel Rampersad, one of the four soldiers who was recently killed in the war and a New York native, was removed from the database. Hochul said, "The Trump administration does not get to revise the human cost of this war because it has become politically inconvenient," and added, "Sgt. Rampersad gave her life in service to this country. Changing a website does not rewrite the truth of her sacrifice."House adopts Iran war powers resolutionThe controversy has also spilled over to Congress. In a rare rebuke of Trump, the House of Representatives last week adopted an Iran war powers resolution, with several Republicans, including Thomas Massie, Warren Davidson, Brian Fitzpatrick, and Tom Barrett, extending their support.In a statement last week, Massie said, "Let me explain this absurd ruse: The Pentagon is pretending there have been two Iran wars separated by a brief cease-fire," and added that Pete Hegseth, the Secretary of Defense, was breaking the law and "must be held accountable" for waging war without Capitol Hill's approval.The revised count came after Trump last week downplayed the human cost of the Iran conflict. In a social media post, he compared the US fatalities in Iran with those in Afghanistan, Iraq, Korea, and Vietnam, wars that spanned years and claimed thousands of US lives.

The Escalatory Escalator

The first option on the table is a calculated campaign of coercion. By inflicting maximum pain through strikes on civilian infrastructure, Washington hopes to force Tehran back to the negotiating table with more favourable terms. The objective here is not victory, but a political “save face” exit for Donald Trump—a deal that allows the administration to declare a win over the “Pick-Axe Mountain” without achieving its original maximalist goals. The problem here is that Iran is refusing to cooperate. The second option is far more aggressive: an uninterrupted missile campaign aimed at fracturing the Iranian state, compelling a total capitulation on regime change, the surrender of enriched uranium stockpiles, and the forfeiture of Iran’s oil revenues. Should these fail, the third option looms—the deployment of ground troops.

However, this final escalation is mired in ambiguity. Strategists are tangled in a debate over who exactly would constitute these ground forces. Would they be American boots on the ground, Israeli special forces, Syrian proxies, or Kurdish militias? The operational reality, however, is starkly simple. At the end of the day, it can, and it will be only American ground troops. This reality comes at an enormous cost in blood and treasure—a cost that would likely define the next phase of the war, following what might be a fleeting “hydration break” in the form of another Memorandum of Understanding.

A War of Attrition

Beneath the tactical posturing lies a brutal war of attrition. This conflict will not be determined solely by who can inflict the most devastation, but by who can withstand the most pain. In this calculus, Iran appears to hold escalatory dominance. With a global economic depression looming and inflation eroding the purchasing power of the American middle class, the US domestic timeline is critically compressed. For a president facing a midterm election, time is a luxury he does not possess. Conversely, for a 6,000-year-old civilisation accustomed to external pressures, time is a weapon. Iran can absorb blows and retaliate with patience, knowing that the political sands in Washington shift far faster than the tectonics of the Persian Gulf.

This reality is already forcing a strategic retreat. The US is being compelled to move its regional bases further away from Iran’s borders. The massive installations in Kuwait and Bahrain are no longer safe; forces are being pushed back toward Jordan. From Jordan, the trajectory of retreat likely leads to Israel. This geographic shrinking of American power illustrates a critical truth: Donald Trump simply does not have the time, the political capital, or the viable options remaining to decisively win this confrontation. He is caught in an escalation trap.

The Globalisation of Conflict

The dangers multiply when we examine the widening theatre of operations. There is a tangible risk that this regional standoff could merge with the Russia-Ukraine war to form a single global conflagration. We have already seen ominous signs, such as the strike on an Iranian vessel and the killing of an Iranian sailor by Ukraine in international waters. Ukraine accuses Iran of supporting Russia, and Iran promises to retaliate. If a resolution to these interconnected conflicts is not reached in time, the fragmentation of the global security order will become complete.

Meanwhile, following the attack on Yemen’s Sanaa Airport by Saudi Arabia, the Houthi movement—a non-naval power—is executing a de facto maritime blockade of a strategic choke point, controlling the very lifeline of global energy supplies. Saudi Arabia has re-entered the fray, but predominantly to save face. However, the Riyadh leadership cannot sustain prolonged punishment. A retaliatory strike on the Aramco facility in the city of Jizan and possible attacks on the Yanbu pipeline infrastructure are likely more than enough to force Saudi Arabia to back off. They cannot take the pain, and are already grappling with significant budgetary issues exacerbated by low oil volatility and the costs of their own ambitious reforms.

The Diplomatic Void and the Shrinking Objectives

Perhaps the most terrifying signal of the direction of the war is the utter absence of a mediator. Unlike the first MOU, which had Islamabad serving as the referee, the current conflict has no negotiator. The warring parties are not even talking to each other. This total communication breakdown is a profound sign of the dangers ahead, rendering any hope or optimism for an agreement far-fetched. We are witnessing a clash of titanic forces: the hubris of a declining superpower against the defiant pride of a 6,000-year-old civilization.

Remarkably, the US has already been forced to scale down its unachievable objectives. The rhetoric of regime change, dismantling the missile program, and seizing nuclear assets has faded. The issue now is simply the Strait of Hormuz. This scaling back is a tacit admission of strategic defeat.

The Political Pivot

As the Iranian front solidifies into a stalemate, the President is pivoting back to his domestic base. For weeks, the focus was exclusively on Iran. Now that the anticipated quick victory has failed to materialize, and with elections drawing near, a new rallying point is needed. The administration is returning to the familiar terrain of sanctions and tariffs to excite the base, shifting the narrative away from a foreign policy quagmire and back to economic nationalism.

The Road Ahead

We are approaching the most dangerous stage of this escalation. Yet, paradoxically, we should expect a temporary ceasefire to hold first. This will not be a peace; it will be a strategic pause—a hydration break for both sides to re-arm, re-assess, and prepare for the next, much more devastating round of escalation. The lack of common ground or a common table means this war will continue to expand until the costs become too high for even the most resolute superpower to bear. For now, the shadows of war grow longer, with no light yet visible at the end of the tunnel.

news.title: Wokeness Made People ‘More Respectful And Empathetic,’ Fuentes Says During Hunter Biden Interview
news.text:
Conservative political commentator Nick Fuentes suggested that the fruits of woke culture isn’t all bad. 

During an interview with Nick Fuentes and Hunter Biden uploaded Friday by YouTuber Andrew Callaghan, the 27-year-old conservative voice suggested that woke culture has had long-term benefits. “I don’t think everything about wokeism was bad. I think genuinely it has made people more respectful and empathetic,” Fuentes told Callaghan on his page “Channel 5 with Andrew Callaghan.”

Nick Fuentes believes WOKE wasn't all bad"I don't think everything about wokeism was bad. I think genuinely it has made people more respectful and empathetic." pic.twitter.com/6SGn0Rb4Gi— Fuentes Updates (@FuentesUpdates) July 24, 2026

“Wokeism had its excesses. Edge-lording also has its excesses … I think we’re at a middle point between saying the edgiest thing we can think of with no regard for anyone and saying ‘everything is racist … you should lose your job,” he said. (RELATED: California Republican Party Plans To Block Candidates Aligned With Nick Fuentes)

An edge-lord is “someone who makes wildly dark and exaggerated statements (as on an internet forum) with the intent of shocking others,” according to Merriam-Webster. 

“We’re finding a middle ground now where maybe it’s tasteful … tastefully offensive in small doses — less is more,” Fuentes said, which made Hunter chuckle. 

“Let’s be honest, twenty years ago, say when I was growing up, I think there was a lot of cruelty and I think there were some hateful attitudes — and I think as time has gone on, the younger generation (and they may not even be left wing, they may not be what you’d consider woke) — I think they are respectful of people who have different ideas or a different way of life or from a different culture.”

“We make jokes all the time that I’m a far-right guy … or some kind of white supremacist and I’m a Mexican,” Fuentes joked. 

Fuentes also garnered online attention when he outlined an array of choice words against those who think the Confederate States of America were on the right side of history during the American Civil War. “These HILLBILLIES killed a million White people so that they could keep black people in America! They’re the least based army OF ALL TIME!!!”

Nick Fuentes GOES OFF on the Confederacy"These HILLBILLIES killed a million White people so that they could KEEP black people in America! They're the least based army OF ALL TIME!!!" pic.twitter.com/AVn8kb8Nb5— Fuentes Updates (@FuentesUpdates) July 16, 2026

Fuentes has a large virtual following of people who tune into his online streams to hear him discuss political issues and current events. 

Back in 2022, Fuentes had dinner with President Donald Trump and rapper Kanye West.

news.title: Pentagon’s official Iran war death toll no longer lists 4 troops killed during renewed fighting
news.text: WASHINGTON — The four American troops killed during renewed fighting between the U.S. and Iran in recent weeks are no longer listed as part of the Iran war death toll in the Pentagon’s official casualty count but have been placed in a new, separate category. It is raising questions about properly counting the impact to U.S. service members as the Trump administration has escalated strikes on Iran in a bid to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while providing little indication of how it intends to wind down a conflict that is unpopular with many Americans. The Defense Casualty Analysis System, which Pentagon officials have repeatedly pointed to as the definitive source on the numbers of dead and wounded from the conflict, removed the four fallen soldiers as well as dozens of wounded troops from its Iran war tally last week. On Sunday, a new category called “Overseas Operations” emerged on the system’s website, listing the four Army deaths by name as well as 207 wounded. It was unclear if all of the wounded were injured in the Iran conflict. U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, referred questions to the Pentagon, which, along with the White House, did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment. Pentagon described earlier changes to the system as ‘data disruptions’ Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez argued Thursday that the drop in casualty figures in the online system was not an effort to hide the growing human toll of the war but rather the result of “anomalies” and “temporary data disruptions” that were being resolved “imminently.” As late as Tuesday, the website was reporting the war’s official toll as 18 killed and 482 wounded. It appeared to reflect that four soldiers had been killed since fighting resumed despite the signing of an interim ceasefire deal last month — three on a base in Jordan that was struck July 17 by Iranian ballistic missiles and drones, and one in Iraq a day later during a controlled detonation of an Iranian drone. Adding further confusion, when the Pentagon announced two of the deaths in Jordan, it said the troops were supporting the U.S. mission to counter the Islamic State militant group. The other two were announced in press releases simply as supporting overseas operations. President Donald Trump has confirmed the total, writing in a Truth Social post on Tuesday that the “Iran Military Conflict” had claimed 18 lives. By Wednesday, the Iran war figures in the Pentagon’s system fell back to 14 dead and 420 wounded. However, a U.S. official told The Associated Press at the time that the actual number of wounded personnel in the war had actually grown to well over 500 troops. The Pentagon’s top spokesman, Sean Parnell, took to social media that day to assert that the reported drop was a “temporary data disruption.” New category lists casualties following date of renewed fighting The U.S. and Israel launched the war in Iran on Feb. 28, and 14 troops were killed in the initial waves of fighting. Washington and Tehran agreed to a ceasefire in April and then signed an interim deal to end the war in mid-June. It was short-lived. Iran struck three merchant vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on July 7 that were transiting along a route near the coast of Oman overseen by the U.S. military. American forces launched strikes in response to the attacks on vessels in the key energy shipping corridor. Trump soon declared that the ceasefire was over. The Pentagon system’s new “Overseas Operations” category says it tallies casualties starting July 7. Since then, the U.S. and Iran have exchanged regular fire in a bid to control the crucial waterway, with the U.S. hitting Iranian targets nightly for nearly two weeks and Tehran responding with attacks on neighboring countries hosting American forces. There have been no strikes for two nights as mediators push for diplomacy. Since the renewed hostilities began, the Pentagon has provided even less information about military strategy and casualties than it did during the first phase of the conflict. The Pentagon has not held a press briefing about the war since early May, and officials at U.S. Central Command have stopped providing casualty updates to reporters. Pentagon officials such as Valdez and Parnell have insisted that the DCAS website is proof of the commitment to transparency about the number of dead and injured in the war.

 Greens target data centres, corporate wealth in bid to win from voter angst 

 Can the Greens capitalise on anxiety about AI and growing inequality – or will a rival snatch the Opportunity? 

 Sam Sachdeva

Analysis: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Newton’s third law may only truly apply to physics, but its allegorical value cannot be entirely dismissed, particularly in the political world.

The growing popularity of New York mayor Zohran Mamdani – far beyond the city he governs – can be in part viewed as a response to Donald Trump’s strongman politics, while in the UK, the rise of Nigel Farage’s Reform has been mirrored by a similar surge in support for the Greens.

Greens take aim at the ‘cost of greed’ with $32b wealth and big tech tax plan 

 Politics 

Green Party chief aims for no more sideshows this election year 

It is a reaction that NZ’s own Green Party wants to see on our own shores, as was evident at the party’s pre-election AGM in Auckland yesterday.

“Every day, powerful men are making decisions to increase the profits of a few at the top, and you pay the price,” Chlöe Swarbrick declared in condemning what she deemed “an extractive economy”, while fellow co-leader Marama Davidson accused the Government of “spitting on communities like those in South Auckland while they cheerlead for the super rich and big corporates”.

The party’s official campaign slogan, ‘For All Of Us’, seems designed to further emphasise the idea that the coalition is governing in the interests of the 1 percent, while pitching the Greens as a welcoming home for voters who feel their parties have abandoned them.

“What we believe very fundamentally is that we’re not just here to fight for the basic human rights to access food and healthcare and shelter and education and job opportunities for the people that we know and like, but also for the people we don’t know – and even those we don’t like,” as Swarbrick put it to media.

The party’s flagship policy from the conference weekend, a one-year moratorium on new AI data centres until proper rules and regulations can be put in place, offers a window into how the party could merge its traditional values with contemporary anxiety about the age we live in.

While the debate over such centres is in a relatively nascent stage here, the backlash is more well developed in the US where critics seize on concerns about their environmental impact – a core Green issue – as well as unease about what the broader AI movement will mean for job security and wealth inequality.

“Only once we have secured an affordable power supply for New Zealanders and the workers building things in towns all across this beautiful country, maybe then we could consider entertaining the expansion of Silicon Valley,” Swarbrick told party members, questioning the Govt for, on the one hand, wringing its hands about the country’s ‘dry year’ problem while simultaneously trying to woo energy-guzzling data centres.

While Christopher Luxon has brushed off calls for a moratorium as “alarmist”, US polling shows concern about the impact of these centres spanning the political divide, suggesting there may be fertile territory for the Greens to explore.

But while the party is showing signs of a slight uptick in support this year, it is having to fight for position with a newcomer eager to break into Parliament – the Opportunity Party.

While both parties are keen to play up their differences, there is clearly some overlap in terms of their potential voter base, so it was unsurprising to see Davidson talking up her party’s long history as an implicit contrast to Opportunity.

“Knowing about our history as the Green Party in Parliament, and the Alliance, and the Values Party before that is crucial to knowing who we are now. The Green Party was forged from social justice and peace movements, environmental movements and climate movements.”

Davidson doubled down in comments to media afterwards, emphasising the Greens’ “longstanding consistency”, before taking a more explicit shot at Opportunity.

“This is a party who have said that they will put this Government – who have spat on the very communities I am accountable to, including South Auckland – they will put that Govt back in power. That is their pathway to power.

“We are focused on being able to say that we can not just kick this Government out, but put in place one that can ensure affordable lives, healthy nature, and honest decisions for all of us.”

Will the Greens’ track record in Parliament, and its willingness to nail its flag to Labour’s mast, prove an asset – or will voters keen for a new approach to politics continue to look Opportunity’s way?

The party won’t have to wait long to see whether Newton’s principles work in its favour.

news.title: Katy Perry hits back at US president Donald Trump as White House uses her song
news.text:
Pop star Katy Perry has hit back at US President Donald Trump for using one of her hit songs in a video showing footage of military strikes.

On Friday, the Trump administration posted a clip on the White House’s official TikTok account that featured missiles exploding.

The post described as a “disgrace” was set to Perry’s 2010 hit song Firework and used her infamous lyrics “boom, boom, boom”. 

Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Arrow

“Iran has been warned,” the video’s caption read.

“I am deeply appalled and angry to see ‘Firework’ used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes,” Perry posted on X. 

“I did not approve this, I was not asked and I absolutely do not condone it.”

Perry said she wrote the song to give people “hope, healing and inner strength” during their darkest days. 

“To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponised to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for,” Perry continued. 

“My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare.”

Perry joins many other musicians — including Céline Dion, Olivia Rodrigo, Sabrina Carpenter and Radiohead — who have told the Trump administration to stop using their music on social media since the beginning of the president’s second term.

Singer Sabrina Carpenter slammed Trump in December last year for using her song in what she called an “evil and disgusting” video.

The Trump administration posted a TikTok showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detaining people during raids across America.

But the footage was set to Carpenter’s 2024 hit song Juno, prompting the pop star to fire back and condemn the use of her music in the clip.

“This video is evil and disgusting,” Carpenter wrote on X at the time. 

“Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”

news.title: Make smoking cool again? Pop culture reboots the vice
news.text: From beauty mogul Kylie Jenner lighting up on the cover of Vanity Fair to cigarette trays at singer Dua Lipa's wedding, the pop culture-verse has rebooted cigarettes as the accessory du jour, health risks be damned. Smoking rates are at a six-decade low among American adults and the lowest in a quarter-century among youth. And yet, searches for the term "smoking pose" on the image-sharing platform Pinterest have soared 70 percent among 18- to 24-year-olds, according to Style Analytics, a fashion world data tracker. On Instagram, the account "Cigfluencers" shares images of celebrities smoking -- "your favorite smoker's favorite smokers," reads the tagline. The posts included a number of shots snapped in May at the Met Gala, the annual gathering of A-listers in New York. Even though current US smoking statistics don't show an increase in the actual habit, making cigarettes chic again has triggered concern among anti-smoking advocates. "Pop culture's glamorization of smoking is just reigniting the addiction among young people and discouraging those trying to quit," Jessica Rath, vice president at the anti-tobacco advocacy group Truth Initiative, told AFP. - 'Highly concerning' - Megan Stalter with a prop cigarette on the red carpet of the 2026 Actor Awards (768x501, AR: 1.53)The organization noted that eight of the 10 feature films nominated for this year's best picture Oscar contained images of tobacco use. This type of exposure makes young people two to three times more likely to use tobacco products, Rath said. Brian King, head of US programs at the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, said the trend is "highly concerning from a public health perspective." One explanation for the resurgence is the return of aesthetics from the 1990s and early 2000s -- an era when smoking was still quite common in the United States. The look was all over the recent popular series "Love Story," a show that detailed the storied relationship of the late John F. Kennedy Jr and Carolyn Bessette -- the latter was a regular smoker and was portrayed as such on the show. The brand strategy newsletter On Brand has dubbed the smoker's aesthetic an act of rebellion against the social media pressures of "self-optimization." And it's all set, of course, against a backdrop of economic and geopolitical uncertainty. "Right now, we're also having kind of a colliding mental health crisis with young people," said Rath. "And so young people are thinking that using nicotine is helping their feelings of anxiety, depression, and stress -- when really it could be making it worse." King noted that public attention has shifted away from the risks associated with conventional cigarettes, as e-cigarettes, heated tobacco products and nicotine pouches grow in popularity. "In some cases, we as society have been recalcitrant in terms of remembering those risks, and also importantly implementing policies that we know work to prevent the use of these products," King said. - 'De-normalize smoking' - US President Donald Trump's administration has made significant cuts to smoking prevention and cessation support programs. And the previous administration under Joe Biden backed off its plan to ban menthol cigarettes, which are popular among young people. King said that in the US, the tobacco industry spends the equivalent of approximately $1 million an hour on marketing and promotion. Nonprofits and anti-smoking organizations lack data on how tobacco companies might be pushing the "cigfluencer" phenomenon. But it's critical, King said, that the United States works to "de-normalize smoking" in the face of such trends. Society must "not be doing anything that could potentially reverse the considerable progress that we've made in reducing smoking over many decades," he said. Along with traditional methods of discouraging smoking -- public service messaging, cessation support, price hikes, and smoking bans -- Rath recommends working with platforms and Hollywood to discourage the habit. She suggests displaying on-screen messages directing viewers to support services, similar to those already in use to prevent suicide or assist those suffering sexual violence. "Shows also have the power to reduce tobacco depictions and incorporate realistic quitting examples into storylines," said Truth Initiative, noting recent depictions in "The Bear" of the main character working to quit smoking using nicotine replacement therapy. pel/mdo/md

news.title: Trump cannot implement mail-in voting order, US appeals court rules
news.text: A federal appeals court on Saturday declined to allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to implement in 23 states an executive order he signed that aims to tighten rules ‌for mail-in voting ahead of November elections that will decide control of Congress.The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the administration's request to lift an injunction several Democratic-led states secured on June 25 from a lower-court judge who concluded that key parts of the Republican president's order were unconstitutional, Reuters reported.In asking the court to pause US District Judge Indira Talwani's ruling while it pursues an appeal, the US Department of Justice had argued that because government agencies had yet to finalize actions and policies to implement Trump's directive, any lawsuit challenging his order was premature. The appeals court, in a 2-1 ruling, rejected that argument."As the district court reasoned, the (executive order) lays out a clear set of rapidly approaching deadlines by which states must coordinate with federal officials and comply with new voting procedures — all while the states must also ensure that their officials and the public understand the evolving set of rules that would govern the upcoming September and November elections," the judges wrote."The Plaintiff States have no practical choice but to respond to the (order) now." Before Talwani ruled, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., rejected a related effort by Democrats to block Trump's order on similar grounds. The Justice Department warned that absent a ruling in its favor from the 1st Circuit, it may be forced to ask the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene.Trump's March orderTrump signed the executive order in March after years of calling for tighter rules on voting by mail and pushing the false claim that his 2020 election defeat was the result of widespread voter fraud. Under the US Constitution, states are assigned the role of administering federal elections.That order came on top of other efforts by Trump to overhaul elections. He has made winning approval in Congress of a divisive package of voting restrictions called the SAVE America Act a priority. Judges have blocked an earlier executive order he signed requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and restricting the counting of mail ballots.The March order directed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to compile and transmit to the states a list of confirmed US citizens eligible to vote in each state, derived from citizenship and naturalisation records and other federal databases. Trump's order also required the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on each state's approved mail-in ballot list. USPS recently moved to implement Trump's directive by issuing new proposed rules requiring states to provide the names and ​barcodes tied to their mail-in ballots.It also directed the US Department of Justice to prioritise the investigation and prosecution of state and local election officials who issue federal ballots to people deemed "not eligible" to vote.But Talwani, in siding with a coalition of 23 states and the District of Columbia that was led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington state, said the president lacked any authority to direct DHS to compile voter eligibility lists for each state to use and that USPS had no statutory authorization to adopt any binding regulations on mail-in voting.The judge, who was appointed by Democratic President Barack Obama, said Trump also could not attempt through his order "to intimidate local election officials to use the necessarily incomplete confirmed citizenship lists as a resource, lest they face criminal prosecution."(With inputs from Reuters)

news.title: Trump refuts claims of dwindling munitions says "have far more than we need": Report
news.text:
Washington, DC [US], July 27 (ANI): US President Donald Trump on Sunday (local time) dismissed growing concerns that military stockpiles are reaching dangerously low levels, directly refuting reports that interceptor shortages are constraining American military strategy in the ongoing conflict with Iran.In a statement to The Wall Street Journal, Trump rejected claims that dwindling munitions pose a problem for US defence capabilities, asserting, "we have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need."The President's remarks come in response to a report by The New York Times regarding internal administration deliberations where Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman General Dan Caine expressed concerns that interceptor reserves could be exhausted if military operations escalate further.According to officials cited by The Wall Street Journal, US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper believes American forces can manage the constrained inventory of Patriot and other air defence interceptors.The strategy relies on expanding US strikes, pending approval from Trump, to neutralise Iran's launching capacity before large-scale missile volleys can be initiated. At the same time, White House officials warned that publishing updated US government figures detailing Patriot and THAAD missile expenditures since the outbreak of hostilities would pose a risk to national security, Wall Street Journal reported. Despite official reluctance to release precise data, The Wall Street Journal highlighted updated estimates by Centre for Strategic and International Studies analysts Mark Cancian and Chris Park, who calculate that at least 1,500 Patriot interceptors have been expended since the conflict began, leaving an estimated inventory of fewer than 1,000 interceptors remaining.In their initial April report analysing key munitions used in the war, Cancian and Park noted that "the diminished munitions stockpiles have created a near-term risk," warning that "a war against a capable peer competitor like China will consume munitions at greater rates than in this war."

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell maintained that the military possesses all necessary resources to execute any mission ordered by the President.The Wall Street Journal reported that the persistent threat from Iranian missile systems was highlighted last week after three Iranian ballistic missiles struck a base in Jordan, resulting in the deaths of three US service members after one missile hit a housing area. While Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the vast majority of incoming missiles targeting the facility were intercepted, US officials told The Wall Street Journal that Iran's military is continually adjusting its tactics by varying flight paths, speeds, and manoeuvres to bypass defence networks, thereby forcing a higher consumption of counter-missile interceptors. The Wall Street Journal also reported growing concern within the Pentagon over regional allies, as Gulf states face similar strains after expending a significant portion of their own air defence interceptor stocks.This comes after The New York Times reported that US President Donald Trump shelved plans for a major military escalation against Iran, opting to hold off on a wider offensive amid growing warnings from defence officials regarding critical shortages in the Pentagon's air defence stockpiles across the Middle East.According to a report by The New York Times, military leaders cautioned that a broader campaign could dangerously deplete supplies of Patriot antimissile interceptors, exposing US troops, Gulf partners, and key installations to retaliatory strikes, while senior aides voiced concern over wider economic instability and escalating regional crises.Private deliberations among top administration officials and military commanders focused heavily on the dwindling inventory of Patriot interceptors and other defensive systems deployed in the region. Concerns intensified after three US service members were killed in Jordan when an enemy ballistic missile penetrated American defences during a barrage of Iranian drones and missiles, a senior US official told The New York Times.General Dan Caine, Chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff, privately advised that while executing major combat operations against Iran remained doable, it would dangerously strain interceptor supplies allocated to US Central Command, the NYT reported, citing officials familiar with the discussions.Meanwhile, in a brief respite following nearly two weeks of intense military action, Iran reported an absence of overnight bombardment on Saturday, signalling an interruption to 13 consecutive nights of American military strikes. (ANI)
